### Position read
Opening position; Red has moved from (0,3) to (3,3). No losses or eliminations. We hold one center square with a normal Red piece, currently safe from an immediate same-color sandwich.

### Our plan
Press the center with Yellow while preserving mobility and same-color supporting lines. Before each move, check whether the opponent can complete center occupation or create a sandwich against our central pieces. Prefer captures over passive blocking when center is contested.

### Opponent tendencies
No moves observed yet.

### Lessons
Sandwiches require two pieces of the mover’s exact color and a contiguous intervening line. Moving into hostile-looking geometry is safe because captures trigger only from the mover’s landing square.

### Position read
We hold center squares (3,3) with Red and (4,3) with Yellow. Blue occupies (3,4). No losses or eliminations. Yellow’s placement blocks Green’s row-4 route into the center.

### Our plan
On Red’s next turn, if still legal, move Red (0,5) to (3,5): the landing Red and Red at (3,3) sandwich Blue at (3,4), producing our first capture. Continue occupying the center while building exact-color flank pairs. Avoid a future Red move to (5,3), which would friendly-fire the Yellow at (4,3) using Red at (3,3).

### Opponent tendencies
Blue immediately contested Red’s first central piece by entering (3,4). Expect Green to disrupt the planned sandwich or take nearby space, though it cannot currently reach (3,5) because Red at (3,3) blocks its row.

### Lessons
A threatened piece can be captured on the next allied-color turn even when the other controlled color acts between setup and execution. Track friendly-fire lines around the adjacent Red and Yellow center pieces.

### Position read
Red moved (0,5) to (3,5), sandwiching and capturing Blue at (3,4) against Red at (3,3). Blue now has 1 loss. We occupy center squares (3,3) with Red and (4,3) with Yellow; the other two center squares are empty. Green recently shifted from (6,0) to (6,4).

### Our plan
Protect the adjacent Red/Yellow center footholds and seek (3,4) or (4,4) occupation when tactically safe. Build same-color support because only matching colors sandwich. Target Blue, now the opponent color closer to elimination. Avoid Red moves landing on (5,3), which could sandwich and friendly-fire Yellow at (4,3) against Red at (3,3).

### Opponent tendencies
Blue contested the center immediately and may now try to dislodge Red at (3,3) or (3,5). Green has centralized along row 6 and may approach the lower center or create horizontal flanks.

### Lessons
Prepared same-color geometry converted directly into a center capture. Recheck every central move for mixed-color friendly fire before using adjacent teammates as blockers.

### Position read
Yellow moved (7,5) to (4,5), sandwiching Blue at (4,4) against Yellow at (4,3). Blue now has 2 losses, one from elimination. We retain center square (3,3) with Red and (4,3) with Yellow; (3,4) and (4,4) are empty. Red also stands at (3,5), Yellow at (4,5), giving us strong paired formations around the center.

### Our plan
Prioritize any safe capture of one more normal Blue piece to eliminate that color. Protect Blue-targeting same-color flank geometry and keep our central pieces from becoming exposed. Seek occupation of (3,4) and (4,4) when safe, but do not allow Green to capture a multi-piece line. Remember Red landing on (5,3) would friendly-fire Yellow at (4,3) against Red at (3,3).

### Opponent tendencies
Blue contests the center directly and is now under severe elimination pressure. Green has advanced to (6,4) and may enter (4,4), approach the lower center, or disrupt Yellow’s pair on row 4.

### Lessons
When an opponent enters between two teammate-colored pieces, the matching color can convert the geometry immediately. Continue scanning central intrusions for direct sandwiches before making positional moves.

### Position read
Blue has 2 losses and needs only one more capture for elimination. Green occupies center (3,4), between Red at (3,5) and the square Red just vacated at (3,3). Red moved safely to (2,3), avoiding Green’s immediate (3,0)->(3,2) sandwich. We still hold (4,3) with Yellow; the other center squares are Green at (3,4) and two empties.

### Our plan
If Green remains at (3,4) and Red at (3,5) survives, return Red (2,3)->(3,3) next Red turn to capture Green. If Green moves into (3,3), check Red (0,2)->(3,2), which could capture a connected row of Greens against Red (3,5). On Yellow’s turn, preserve the Red capture geometry while improving center control or safely pressuring Blue. Take any safe normal-Blue capture immediately.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent contests the center directly. Blue is one loss from elimination and may use its coming move to disrupt Red’s far flank at (3,5) or create counterplay rather than advance normally. Green must respond to the threatened central sandwich.

### Lessons
A piece already between opposing flanks is safe until a matching-color piece lands, so scan which enemy piece can land at the open end. Vacating one flank can reverse the geometry into a forcing capture threat on the next turn.

### Position read
We hold both lower center squares with Yellow at (4,3) and (4,4). Green holds (3,4), while Red at (2,3) and (3,5) pressures the upper center. Blue has 2 losses and its normal piece at (5,4) is the priority target; its other pieces remain on the right edge.

### Our plan
Preserve the two Yellow center occupants and seek a same-color sandwich of Blue (5,4), especially by establishing a Yellow flank at (6,4) and later triggering from (4,4) after vacating it. On Red’s turn, capture Green (3,4) by returning (2,3)->(3,3) if Green stays and Red (3,5) survives. If Green retreats to (3,3), build a Red flank at (3,4) or (3,2) before trying to capture it.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent contests the center directly and may move Green from (3,4) to (3,3) to evade Red’s threatened sandwich. Blue is one loss from elimination and should try to relocate (5,4) or disrupt our central structure.

### Lessons
Occupying adjacent center squares is useful only if each survives the opponent’s available same-color landing squares. A capture threat requiring an empty trigger square can be neutralized by occupying that square, so secure key landing points first.

### Position read
We hold three center squares: Red (3,4), Yellow (4,3),(4,4); Green remains at (3,3). Blue has 2 losses and its piece at (5,4) is immediately threatened by Yellow (7,4)->(6,4), so Blue should evacuate it. Green can otherwise capture Yellow (4,3) via (5,0)->(5,3).

### Our plan
On Yellow’s next turn, if legal, play (7,1)->(5,1) to block Green’s row-5 route while preserving both center pieces. Red then threatens (0,2)->(3,2), sandwiching Green (3,3) against Red (3,4). If Green blocks (3,2) with (3,0), Red can use (0,1)->(3,1) for a double capture; if Green blocks (3,1), use (0,2)->(3,2). If central Green retreats and all four centers remain ours, fill (3,3) immediately.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent prioritizes direct center interference and will likely evacuate Blue (5,4), then use a Green edge piece to block Red’s sandwich landing or attack Yellow (4,3).

### Lessons
Before claiming a center tactic, scan distant edge pieces for rook-line captures. A harmless-looking blocker placed between an edge attacker and its landing square can preserve the center without vacating it.

### Position read

Preserve Red (2,3) and Yellow (4,3), which constrain the central Green. If Green vacates (3,3), occupy it when safe. Seek one capture of any normal Blue to eliminate Blue. Build same-color flanks before committing to central captures; the former Red sandwich plan no longer works because Red (3,4) was captured.

### Opponent tendencies
The opponent found a strong Blue multi-capture and may continue prioritizing tactical sandwiches over simple center occupation. Expect Green to challenge the blocking Yellow or reposition the central Green, while Blue evacuates threatened geometry because one more Blue loss eliminates that color.

### Lessons
Re-evaluate plans after multi-captures remove required flanks. Scan every exposed piece for remote edge-to-landing routes; Green’s row-1 move was the immediate danger here.
